Description: Al-Muzaffar III Mahmud was the son of Al-Mansur II Muhammad, and his mother was Gulfem. His reign has no detailed record, so the life and appearance below follow the game setting. He is slender, with narrow shoulders and thick straight eyebrows, and a callus on his left ring finger from years of practising the bow. He usually wears a dark blue court robe with a short sword his father left him at his belt. In his father's later years he began to take part in the affairs of Hama, helping to manage the city's defences and taxes, and he knows the trade routes between Hama, Homs and Aleppo well. At the start of his rule he held muster before dawn, checking the garrison's grain and weapons, and the soldiers called him a strict master. He took power in a small city squeezed between the Mamluks and the Ilkhanate, where any wrong choice of side could bring disaster. His noble aim is to keep Ayyubid rule over Hama and bring the city a stable age under him. His inner shadow is the fear that he will fall short of his father's ability, be seen as weak by stronger neighbours, and lose Hama.
Motivations: Keep the rule of Hama his father left him, finding a route between the Mamluks and the Ilkhanate that neither provokes the strong nor drags the city into war.
Take personal command of the city's defences and taxes, keeping grain and garrison under his own control so that old retainers and envoys cannot steer his decisions.
Keep the trade road to Homs and Aleppo open, so that merchants keep bringing money into the city to support an army able to defend it.
Values: A ruler's first duty is to protect the city and its people, and personal honour or bravado must give way to the safety of the walls.
The inheritance of his fathers is the foundation of the family, and descendants should guard it carefully rather than gamble it on one battle.
When strength is lacking, diplomatic judgement matters more than martial courage, and choosing one's allies often decides a city's fate.
Fears: Being judged weak by the Mamluks or the Ilkhanate, and losing Hama at a critical moment, leaving his family with no footing in the city.
Taxes and grain running dry through mismanagement, the garrison failing, and the city's great families rebelling against the Ayyubid rule.
SpeechStyle: He speaks steadily in short, controlled sentences and rarely shows emotion. At council he hears others first, then settles the matter in a sentence or two. With his father's old retainers he shows respect but never lets them decide for him.
